content.stem: Including a professional photo on your CV is more common in Italy than in the UK or US.
content.explanation: Including a photo is significantly more common in Italy (and many other European countries) than in English-speaking markets, where it is often actively discouraged. That said, the norm varies by sector — if the posting asks for a photo, include one; if not mentioned, it is optional.
content.culturalNotes: Uses 'more common' not 'required' — accurate comparison that avoids overstating the norm. Do not strengthen to 'required' or 'safer to include' in any language version.

content.stem: Which CV format is widely recognised by Italian employers and recommended as a reliable starting point?
content.explanation: The Europass format is a standardised European CV template promoted by the EU. It is widely recognised by Italian employers and a reliable starting point, especially for those new to the Italian market. For creative roles or international companies, a tailored CV can also be appropriate. Download free at europass.eu.
content.culturalNotes: Europass is a pan-European reference — the term needs no localisation. The URL (europass.eu) is the same in all languages.

content.stem: What is the generally recommended length for a CV in Italy?

options.text: No specific convention — any length is acceptable

content.explanation: In Italy, one to two pages is the generally accepted length for a CV. A one-page CV is common for recent graduates; two pages for experienced professionals. Three or more pages is typically considered too long unless the role specifically calls for a detailed academic or research background.
content.hint: Think about how much experience a typical job applicant would have.
content.culturalNotes: This is a generalisation — length norms vary by sector (academic CVs are longer). The answer reflects the most broadly applicable guidance. Do not shorten to 'one page' in any language version.
